Photograph: Olympia de Maismont/AFP/Getty Images Nigeria Almost 50 dead in Nigeria after drinking alcohol suspected to contain methanol Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated Associated Press Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least 48 people have died and about 100 others are receiving treatment in southern Nigeria after consuming a locally brewed alcoholic concoction suspected to contain methanol, officials said on Thursday. Banji Ajaka, Ondo state’s commissioner for health, said the cases had been reported in the Odigbo and Irele local government areas. A total of 182 people are believed to have been affected and some are being treated in the hospital, he said. “I took like two shots and I went out on Friday. On Saturday, I noticed that I could not see,” 32-year-old Sola Adebayo told the local TVC News channel from a hospital bed. ‘At 2am, it feels like someone’s there’: why Nigerians are choosing chatbots to give them advice and therapy Read more Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated. “This thing happened rapidly. Once they consume, depending on the quantity, the kidneys will pack up, the eyes will go, the brain will be damaged,” Ajaka told The Associated Press, speaking about the drink. Ondo state police spokesperson Abayomi Jimoh said in a statement that 15 people were arrested in connection with the incident, including one allegedly “involved in the production of substances suspected to contain methanol and is currently assisting the police with investigations.” Locals told the AP they suspected a popular herbal drink with high alcohol content, known as “Monkey Tail,” was mixed with methanol, causing the deaths. A trader who sells the concoction in Odigbo, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of being arrested, told the AP there are two versions of Monkey Tail: an original, safe version, and another version which is unsafe. Local media reports said the first death was reported nearly two weeks ago. Nigeria’s National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control is now enforcing a nationwide ban on alcohol in sachets and small plastic containers, which it said are easily accessible to children and young people. Blame Russia: Finnish president takes page from NATO chief's playbook RT.com 05 Oct 2026, 09:39 GMT+10 Alexander Stubb has linked Moscow to a range of EU troubles while maintaining that a direct conflict is unlikely Finnish President Alexander Stubb has blamed Russia for a wide range of security concerns facing the EU, including the influx of migrants into Ceuta, Spain's enclave in Morocco, over the summer. He later admitted that he did not know the situation in Ceuta well enough to take a position. Stubb made the remarks in an interview with Spanish newspaper El Mundo over the weekend. When asked about potential hybrid threats posed by Moscow, Stubb claimed that Russia would try to interfere with the upcoming Spanish elections. Madrid "should expect some form of sabotage or hybrid attack. It could be related to information warfare or a campaign that threatens their democracy," he stated. The president went on to claim that Russian-backed cyberattacks were "happening, as we speak, against Spanish banks and other targets," without citing specific evidence. "They send asylum seekers to our border, as we have also seen in Ceuta," he said, accusing Moscow of committing acts of sabotage throughout the EU. He also mentioned cases in which Russian-linked ships were accused of cutting undersea telecommunications cables in the Baltic Sea and the recent incident at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport, where explosive-laden drones were found near Ukrainian cargo planes. Germany blamed Moscow and ordered the closure of a Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural center in Berlin. Russia dismissed the accusations as "nonsensical" and denied any involvement in the incident. When pressed further about Russia's alleged role in the Ceuta crisis in late July, when more than 70,000 migrants irregularly crossed into the enclave, Stubb admitted that he did not "know the matter well enough to take a position." Reuters reported at the time that migrants had been encouraged by viral videos and misleading claims about Spain's asylum and migration rules. Spain later accused Russian- and Israeli-linked networks of spreading disinformation surrounding the crisis, allegations both countries denied. Stubb's interview came after NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte encouraged members of the bloc to publicly attribute incidents to Russia when they were certain, or "almost sure," that Moscow was responsible. "When able, when you are sure it is the Russians, or almost sure it is the Russians, attribute it to the Russians," Rutte told a press conference this week. Direct conflict unlikely At the same time, when asked about the possibility of a direct conflict between NATO and Russia, Stubb dismissed the immediate risk as negligible. "Do we expect Russia to attack? The answer is no. We have no evidence of that," he told El Mundo. According to the Finnish president, EU leaders themselves have a "communication problem," as some have been "acting in an alarmist way and conflating [hypothetical] scenarios with the perception of the threat." In a similar vein, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius urged officials this week not to "exaggerate" when making alarmist statements about Russia and said there was no evidence that Moscow was planning an attack on NATO. Rutte has also said that there was "no imminent threat to NATO territory." Nevertheless, EU officials have argued that the bloc, as well as NATO, should be prepared for a potential clash with Russia, with German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius saying that the country must be ready for a conflict as early as 2028. The German government amended its constitutional debt brake to fund military spending and passed a 2026 budget allocating a record 108.2 billion ($121.5 billion) to defense and 11.5 billion in military assistance for Ukraine. Russia has repeatedly said that it would not attack NATO unless attacked first. Moscow has warned, however, that Western military aid to Ukraine makes a dangerous escalation more likely. President Vladimir Putin has argued that European politicians are stirring tensions with Moscow to distract voters from economic and political problems at home.
